Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $\Theta$ be a parameter set,
and for each $\theta\in\Theta$ let $E_\theta:X\to\mathbb R$ be a measurable
energy function. Its **partition function relative to $\mu$** is
$$Z_\theta:=\int_X e^{-E_\theta(x)}\,d\mu(x).$$
The admissible parameter set is
$$\Theta_\mu:=\{\theta\in\Theta:0<Z_\theta<\infty\}.$$
For $\theta\in\Theta_\mu$, the **energy-based probability measure** is the
measure with density $e^{-E_\theta}/Z_\theta$ relative to $\mu$:
$$P_\theta(A):=\frac{1}{Z_\theta}\int_A e^{-E_\theta(x)}\,d\mu(x),\qquad A\in\mathcal A.$$
The restriction $0<Z_\theta<\infty$ is part of the definition; parameters
outside $\Theta_\mu$ do not define a normalized model by this formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
For every real $x$, the series $\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/\iota(n!)$ converges absolutely. Its power-series radius is therefore $+\infty$.
If $f(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_n(x-c)^n$ for $|x-c|<R$, then $f$ is continuous at every $x_0$ satisfying $|x_0-c|<R$.

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then
$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

derivations.claim: Define $\phi(t):=\exp(-t)$. By [F4], $\phi(t)=\sum_{n\ge0}(-1)^nt^n/\iota(n!)$ is a power-series sum with infinite radius, so [F5] makes $\phi$ continuous on $\mathbb R$. Thus [F6] makes it Borel measurable, and [F7] with the measurable energy from [F1] makes $x\mapsto\exp(-E_\theta(x))$ measurable. Its values are positive by [F8], hence nonnegative. Put $M_\theta(A):=\int_A e^{-E_\theta}\,d\mu$. Now [F2] makes $M_\theta$ a measure and $M_\theta(X)=Z_\theta$. Thus $P_\theta(\varnothing)=Z_\theta^{-1}M_\theta(\varnothing)=0$. For any pairwise disjoint sequence $(A_n)_{n\ge0}$, [F2] and finite-sum homogeneity give $P_\theta(\bigcup_{n\ge0}A_n)=Z_\theta^{-1}\sum_{n\ge0}M_\theta(A_n)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{n=0}^N Z_\theta^{-1}M_\theta(A_n)=\sum_{n\ge0}P_\theta(A_n)$. Therefore $P_\theta$ is a measure.
Its total mass is $P_\theta(X)=Z_\theta^{-1}M_\theta(X)=1$, so [F3] makes $P_\theta$ a probability measure.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $\Theta$ be a parameter set,
and for each $\theta\in\Theta$ let $E_\theta:X\to\mathbb R$ be a measurable
energy function. Its **partition function relative to $\mu$** is
$$Z_\theta:=\int_X e^{-E_\theta(x)}\,d\mu(x).$$
The admissible parameter set is
$$\Theta_\mu:=\{\theta\in\Theta:0<Z_\theta<\infty\}.$$
For $\theta\in\Theta_\mu$, the **energy-based probability measure** is the
measure with density $e^{-E_\theta}/Z_\theta$ relative to $\mu$:
$$P_\theta(A):=\frac{1}{Z_\theta}\int_A e^{-E_\theta(x)}\,d\mu(x),\qquad A\in\mathcal A.$$
The restriction $0<Z_\theta<\infty$ is part of the definition; parameters
outside $\Theta_\mu$ do not define a normalized model by this formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is
**continuously differentiable**, or of class $C^1$, when it is totally
differentiable at every point of $U$ and the entries of its derivative matrix
are continuous functions on $U$.

For an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $a\in U$, a **local inverse of $f$ at
$a$** is a function $g:W\to V$ for open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$
and $f(a)\in W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective and
$g=(f|_V)^{-1}$. If both $f|_V$ and $g$ are $C^1$, this restriction is a
**local diffeomorphism** at $a$.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let
$u,v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and let
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ be the multi-index of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. We say that $v$ is
the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Both integrals are finite because the test and all its derivatives are bounded
and compactly supported. The test identity is choice-free. By
[[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]] and the signed
transpose convention in [[def-distributional-derivative]], it is equivalent
to $\partial^\alpha T_u=T_v$ as distributions. For $\alpha=0$, this identity
reduces to $T_u=T_v$, hence to $u=v$ almost everywhere by the published
embedding theorem under [[def-countable-choice]].

**Well-definedness.** Changing either representative on a null set leaves each
test integral unchanged. Weak derivatives are therefore statements about
almost-everywhere classes; existence and uniqueness of their locally
integrable value classes are audited separately.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$,
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, and $u,v,w\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$. If both
$v$ and $w$ are weak $\alpha$-derivatives of $u$, then
$$v=w\quad\text{almost everywhere on }\Omega.$$
Thus a weak derivative, when it exists, is unique as an almost-everywhere
class. No connectedness assumption is needed.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the assertion holds because there is only the zero
class and no nonzero tests.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $r$ be a positive
integer and $\theta\in\mathbb R^r$,
and let $E_\theta:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable in $x$ and continuously
differentiable in $\theta$. Define the energy model $P_\theta$ relative to $\mu$
only when
$$0<Z_\theta:=\int_\mathcal X e^{-E_\theta(x)}\,d\mu(x)<\infty,$$
with density $e^{-E_\theta}/Z_\theta$. Let $Q_0$ be a data probability
measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and let $K_\theta$ be a probability kernel
from $\mathcal X$ to itself which leaves $P_\theta$ invariant, meaning
$$\int_\mathcal X K_\theta(x,A)\,P_\theta(dx)=P_\theta(A)\qquad(A\in\mathcal A).$$
Let $\{*\}$ carry its full sigma-algebra, let $G_{0,\theta}(*,A):=Q_0(A)$,
and recursively compose the probability kernel $G_{j,\theta}$ from $\{*\}$ to
$\mathcal X$ with $K_\theta$ to obtain $G_{j+1,\theta}$. Define
$Q_{j,\theta}(A):=G_{j,\theta}(*,A)$; thus $Q_{0,\theta}=Q_0$ and
$$Q_{j+1,\theta}(A)=\int_\mathcal X K_\theta(x,A)\,Q_{j,\theta}(dx),\qquad A\in\mathcal A.$$
Finite probability-kernel composition makes each $Q_{j,\theta}$ a probability
measure. For an integer $k\ge1$, $Q_{k,\theta}$ is the $k$-step reconstruction law.

If $Q_0$ and $Q_{k,\theta}$ have specified nonnegative measurable densities
$r_{0,\theta}$ and $r_{k,\theta}$ relative to $P_\theta$, meaning
$Q_{j,\theta}(A)=\int_A r_{j,\theta}\,dP_\theta$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
for $j\in\{0,k\}$, and
$$\int|r_{j,\theta}\log r_{j,\theta}|\,dP_\theta<\infty\qquad(j\in\{0,k\}),$$
define their finite contrastive-divergence objective by
$$\operatorname{CD}_k(\theta):=\int r_{0,\theta}\log r_{0,\theta}\,dP_\theta-\int r_{k,\theta}\log r_{k,\theta}\,dP_\theta,$$
where $0\log0:=0$ and $\log$ is the natural logarithm. On a finite state
space where $P_\theta$ has positive mass at every state, write
$p_\theta(x):=P_\theta(\{x\})$ and $q_{j,\theta}(x):=Q_{j,\theta}(\{x\})$.
Then $r_{j,\theta}(x)=q_{j,\theta}(x)/p_\theta(x)$ and the objective equals
$$\sum_{x:q_{0,\theta}(x)>0}q_{0,\theta}(x)\log\frac{q_{0,\theta}(x)}{p_\theta(x)}-\sum_{x:q_{k,\theta}(x)>0}q_{k,\theta}(x)\log\frac{q_{k,\theta}(x)}{p_\theta(x)},$$
since each finite-space integral is the sum of the integrand times the point
mass and $p_\theta r_{j,\theta}=q_{j,\theta}$.

For a positive integer $m$, the procedure takes independent data draws
$x^1,\ldots,x^m$ with common law $Q_0$, a transition sampler for $K_\theta$,
and a learning rate $\eta>0$; the
reconstruction chains are drawn independently conditional on their starts. Its
output is the updated parameter from the **stop-gradient CD-$k$ update**:

1. For each $i$, set $x^{i,0}=x^i$ and draw $x^{i,j+1}$ from
   $K_\theta(x^{i,j},\cdot)$ for $j=0,\ldots,k-1$.
2. Form
   $$\widehat g_k=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\left(\nabla_\theta E_\theta(x^i)-\nabla_\theta E_\theta(x^{i,k})\right).$$
3. Update $\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\widehat g_k$.

When $\nabla_\theta E_\theta$ is integrable under $Q_0$ and $Q_{k,\theta}$,
the associated **population CD-$k$ direction** is
$$g_k(\theta):=\int\nabla_\theta E_\theta\,dQ_0-\int\nabla_\theta E_\theta\,dQ_{k,\theta}.$$
The procedure makes no claim that the chain has mixed in $k$ steps. The
parameter derivative of $Q_{k,\theta}$ is not stopped in the scalar objective's
definition; the update above deliberately omits that derivative.

Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty set. A **probability vector** on
$\mathcal X$ is a family $P=(p_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$ of real numbers such that
$p_x\ge 0$ for every $x$ and $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_x=1$. Its support is
$\operatorname{supp}P:=\{x\in\mathcal X:p_x>0\}$. Coordinates outside the
support are retained as zeros; they are not deleted from the alphabet.

For another probability vector $Q=(q_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$, the notation
$P\ll Q$ means $\operatorname{supp}P\subseteq\operatorname{supp}Q$. All
finite sums over $\mathcal X$ use the displayed alphabet and ordinary finite
real arithmetic, extended to $+\infty$ only where a later definition says so.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

Since $\mathcal X$ is finite and each energy is real, [F13] makes every $e^{-E_\theta(x)}$ positive; hence [F1] gives $0<Z_\theta<\infty$. The formula for $p_\theta$ then gives positive coordinates summing to one, so it is a probability vector by [F4]. By [F6], [F7] and [F8], differentiating the finite sum gives $\partial_jZ_\theta=-\sum_xe^{-E_\theta(x)}\partial_jE_\theta(x)$. The same chain and quotient rules give $\partial_jp_\theta(x)/p_\theta(x)=-\partial_jE_\theta(x)-\partial_jZ_\theta/Z_\theta=-\partial_jE_\theta(x)+\sum_yp_\theta(y)\partial_jE_\theta(y)$; [F9] identifies the left side with $\partial_j\log p_\theta(x)$. Because $q_0$ is fixed and sums to one by [F4], differentiating $\mathcal L=-\sum_xq_0(x)\log p_\theta(x)$ and summing this identity yields the displayed likelihood-gradient formula.

The recurrence in [F2] gives $q_{j+1,\theta}=q_{j,\theta}K_\theta$, hence $q_{k,\theta}=q_0K_\theta^k$ and $\sum_xq_{k,\theta}(x)=1$. For $k=1$ the product rule [F6] gives $\partial_j(q_0K_\theta)=q_0\partial_jK_\theta$. If $\partial_j(q_0K_\theta^k)=\sum_{s=0}^{k-1}q_0K_\theta^s(\partial_jK_\theta)K_\theta^{k-1-s}$, then entrywise application of [F6] to $q_0K_\theta^kK_\theta$ yields $\sum_{s=0}^{k-1}q_0K_\theta^s(\partial_jK_\theta)K_\theta^{k-s}+q_0K_\theta^k(\partial_jK_\theta)$, which is the same formula with $k+1$ by appending the $s=k$ term. Thus the stated product derivative holds for every $k$. Differentiating $\sum_xq_{k,\theta}(x)=1$ by [F6] gives $\sum_x\partial_jq_{k,\theta}(x)=0$. Strict positivity of $K_\theta$ and nonzero mass of $q_0$ imply $q_{k,\theta}(x)>0$ for every $x$, so the following logarithms are finite.

By the quotient rule [F6], $\partial_j(q_{k,\theta}(x)/p_\theta(x))=\partial_jq_{k,\theta}(x)/p_\theta(x)-q_{k,\theta}(x)\partial_jp_\theta(x)/p_\theta(x)^2$; the chain and logarithm derivative rules [F7, F9] then give $\partial_j\log(q_{k,\theta}(x)/p_\theta(x))=\partial_jq_{k,\theta}(x)/q_{k,\theta}(x)-\partial_j\log p_\theta(x)$. Applying the product rule [F6] to each summand of $D_{\rm KL}(q_{k,\theta}\|p_\theta)$ therefore gives $\partial_jq_{k,\theta}(x)(\log(q_{k,\theta}(x)/p_\theta(x))+1)-q_{k,\theta}(x)\partial_j\log p_\theta(x)$. Summing the finite terms, the $+1$ contribution vanishes by step 1.2. Substitution from step 1.1 yields $\partial_jD_{\rm KL}(q_{k,\theta}\|p_\theta)=\sum_x\partial_jq_{k,\theta}(x)\log(q_{k,\theta}(x)/p_\theta(x))+\sum_xq_{k,\theta}(x)\partial_jE_\theta(x)-\sum_xp_\theta(x)\partial_jE_\theta(x)$.

Since $q_0$ is fixed, the terms $q_0(x)\log q_0(x)$ in $D_{\rm KL}(q_0\|p_\theta)$ have zero derivative; applying the same product and logarithm rules [F6, F9] and using the log-density formula from step 1.1 and $\sum_xq_0(x)=1$ gives $\partial_jD_{\rm KL}(q_0\|p_\theta)=\sum_xq_0(x)\partial_jE_\theta(x)-\sum_xp_\theta(x)\partial_jE_\theta(x)$. Subtracting step 2.1 cancels the model expectations and yields the stated $\partial_j\operatorname{CD}_k$ formula. By [F3], the algorithm uses only its first two terms; the remaining sum is the derivative through $K_\theta^k$. Comparing with step 1.1 also shows that the algorithm replaces the exact likelihood negative phase $p_\theta$ by $q_{k,\theta}$.

Put $w(x_0,\ldots,x_k):=q_0(x_0)\prod_{s=0}^{k-1}K_\theta(x_s,x_{s+1})$. These weights are nonnegative. Summing successively over $x_k,\ldots,x_1$ and using the row sums of $K_\theta$ reduces $\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)$ to $\sum_{x_0}q_0(x_0)=1$. The set function $\mathbb P_\theta(A)=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega)$ vanishes on the empty set and is countably additive: a disjoint sequence of subsets of finite $\Omega$ has only finitely many nonempty terms. Thus [F10] makes it a measure, and [F11] makes it a probability measure.

For $s=0$, $K_\theta^0=I$ is row-stochastic and its entries are the length-zero path weights. If the entries of $K_\theta^s$ sum the products along all length-$s$ paths, then $K_\theta^{s+1}(x,y)=\sum_zK_\theta^s(x,z)K_\theta(z,y)$ appends the final transition, so its entries sum the length-$(s+1)$ path weights; also $\sum_yK_\theta^{s+1}(x,y)=\sum_zK_\theta^s(x,z)\sum_yK_\theta(z,y)=1$. Thus $\mathbb P_\theta(X_0=x,X_k=y)=q_0(x)K_\theta^k(x,y)$. The function $g_f$ is finite-valued; for each Borel $C\subseteq\mathbb R$, $\{g_f(X_0)\in C\}=X_0^{-1}(\{x:g_f(x)\in C\})$, so $g_f(X_0)$ is $\sigma(X_0)$-measurable. Both $f(X_k)$ and $g_f(X_0)$ are integrable since $\Omega$ is finite.

Every event in $\sigma(X_0)$ has the form $\{X_0\in B\}$ for some $B\subseteq\mathcal X$, since these preimages form a sigma-algebra and generate $\sigma(X_0)$. and for each $\theta\in\Theta$ let $E_\theta:X\to\mathbb R$ be a measurable

$$Z_\theta:=\int_X e^{-E_\theta(x)}\,d\mu(x).$$
The admissible parameter set is
$$\Theta_\mu:=\{\theta\in\Theta:0<Z_\theta<\infty\}.$$
For $\theta\in\Theta_\mu$, the **energy-based probability measure** is the
measure with density $e^{-E_\theta}/Z_\theta$ relative to $\mu$:
$$P_\theta(A):=\frac{1}{Z_\theta}\int_A e^{-E_\theta(x)}\,d\mu(x),\qquad A\in\mathcal A.$$
The restriction $0<Z_\theta<\infty$ is part of the definition; parameters
outside $\Theta_\mu$ do not define a normalized model by this formula.

integer and $\theta\in\mathbb R^r$,

differentiable in $\theta$. Define the energy model $P_\theta$ relative to $\mu$
only when
$$0<Z_\theta:=\int_\mathcal X e^{-E_\theta(x)}\,d\mu(x)<\infty,$$
with density $e^{-E_\theta}/Z_\theta$. Let $Q_0$ be a data probability
measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and let $K_\theta$ be a probability kernel
from $\mathcal X$ to itself which leaves $P_\theta$ invariant, meaning
$$\int_\mathcal X K_\theta(x,A)\,P_\theta(dx)=P_\theta(A)\qquad(A\in\mathcal A).$$
Let $\{*\}$ carry its full sigma-algebra, let $G_{0,\theta}(*,A):=Q_0(A)$,
and recursively compose the probability kernel $G_{j,\theta}$ from $\{*\}$ to
$\mathcal X$ with $K_\theta$ to obtain $G_{j+1,\theta}$. Define
$Q_{j,\theta}(A):=G_{j,\theta}(*,A)$; thus $Q_{0,\theta}=Q_0$ and
$$Q_{j+1,\theta}(A)=\int_\mathcal X K_\theta(x,A)\,Q_{j,\theta}(dx),\qquad A\in\mathcal A.$$
Finite probability-kernel composition makes each $Q_{j,\theta}$ a probability
measure. For an integer $k\ge1$, $Q_{k,\theta}$ is the $k$-step reconstruction law.

If $Q_0$ and $Q_{k,\theta}$ have specified nonnegative measurable densities
$r_{0,\theta}$ and $r_{k,\theta}$ relative to $P_\theta$, meaning
$Q_{j,\theta}(A)=\int_A r_{j,\theta}\,dP_\theta$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
for $j\in\{0,k\}$, and
$$\int|r_{j,\theta}\log r_{j,\theta}|\,dP_\theta<\infty\qquad(j\in\{0,k\}),$$
define their finite contrastive-divergence objective by
$$\operatorname{CD}_k(\theta):=\int r_{0,\theta}\log r_{0,\theta}\,dP_\theta-\int r_{k,\theta}\log r_{k,\theta}\,dP_\theta,$$
where $0\log0:=0$ and $\log$ is the natural logarithm. On a finite state
space where $P_\theta$ has positive mass at every state, write
$p_\theta(x):=P_\theta(\{x\})$ and $q_{j,\theta}(x):=Q_{j,\theta}(\{x\})$.

$$\sum_{x:q_{0,\theta}(x)>0}q_{0,\theta}(x)\log\frac{q_{0,\theta}(x)}{p_\theta(x)}-\sum_{x:q_{k,\theta}(x)>0}q_{k,\theta}(x)\log\frac{q_{k,\theta}(x)}{p_\theta(x)},$$
since each finite-space integral is the sum of the integrand times the point
mass and $p_\theta r_{j,\theta}=q_{j,\theta}$.

For a positive integer $m$, the procedure takes independent data draws
$x^1,\ldots,x^m$ with common law $Q_0$, a transition sampler for $K_\theta$,
and a learning rate $\eta>0$; the
reconstruction chains are drawn independently conditional on their starts. Its
output is the updated parameter from the **stop-gradient CD-$k$ update**:

   $K_\theta(x^{i,j},\cdot)$ for $j=0,\ldots,k-1$.
2. Form
   $$\widehat g_k=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\left(\nabla_\theta E_\theta(x^i)-\nabla_\theta E_\theta(x^{i,k})\right).$$
3. Update $\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\widehat g_k$.

parameter derivative of $Q_{k,\theta}$ is not stopped in the scalar objective's
definition; the update above deliberately omits that derivative.

$K_\theta^0=I$, $K_\theta^{s+1}=K_\theta^sK_\theta$, and
$q_{k,\theta}=q_0K_\theta^k$, where vectors are row vectors, and
$$\mathcal L(\theta):=-\sum_xq_0(x)\log p_\theta(x),\qquad \operatorname{CD}_k(\theta):=D_{\rm KL}(q_0\|p_\theta)-D_{\rm KL}(q_{k,\theta}\|p_\theta),$$
where for finite probability mass functions $a,b$ with $b(x)>0$,
$$D_{\rm KL}(a\|b):=\sum_{x:a(x)>0}a(x)\log\frac{a(x)}{b(x)}$$
with $\log$ the natural logarithm and zero-mass terms contributing zero. For each parameter coordinate $j$,
$$\partial_j\mathcal L(\theta)=\sum_xq_0(x)\partial_jE_\theta(x)-\sum_xp_\theta(x)\partial_jE_\theta(x),$$
while
$$\partial_j\operatorname{CD}_k(\theta)=\sum_xq_0(x)\partial_jE_\theta(x)-\sum_xq_{k,\theta}(x)\partial_jE_\theta(x)-\sum_x\partial_jq_{k,\theta}(x)\log\frac{q_{k,\theta}(x)}{p_\theta(x)}.$$
The reconstruction-law derivative is
$$\partial_jq_{k,\theta}=\sum_{s=0}^{k-1}q_0K_\theta^s(\partial_jK_\theta)K_\theta^{k-1-s}.$$
Thus the population direction used by stop-gradient CD-$k$ is the first two
terms of the displayed $\partial_j\operatorname{CD}_k$ formula and omits the
explicit derivative through the $k$ transition kernels. It also replaces the
model expectation in the exact negative log-likelihood gradient by the finite
reconstruction law; no equality between these gradients is asserted.

For the finite-state path calculation, let $\Omega:=\mathcal X^{k+1}$ with its
full sigma-algebra, let $X_s$ be the $s$th coordinate map, and define
$$\mathbb P_\theta(A):=\sum_{(x_0,\ldots,x_k)\in A}q_0(x_0)\prod_{s=0}^{k-1}K_\theta(x_s,x_{s+1}),\qquad A\subseteq\Omega.$$
This is a probability measure. For every real $f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$, set
$$g_f(x):=\begin{cases}\sum_yK_\theta^k(x,y)f(y),&q_0(x)>0,\\0,&q_0(x)=0.\end{cases}$$
Then $g_f(X_0)$ is a version of
$\mathbb E_{\mathbb P_\theta}[f(X_k)\mid\sigma(X_0)]$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.
